item.title: Constrained Sparsest Input Selection for Structural Controllability is NP-Hard
item.description: arXiv:2610.31195v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the problem of selecting the fewest admissible input--state links that make a structured linear system structurally controllable. This objective counts nonzero entries from prescribed positions of the input matrix and is different from minimizing its number of nonzero columns. Prior work gives polynomial-time algorithms for several restricted cases, including single or dedicated inputs and prescribed input patterns satisfying additional graph-theoretic conditions. We give a polynomial-time reduction from perfect three-dimensional matching, establishing for the first time that the decision problem is NP-complete and the optimization problem is NP-hard. A refinement of the reduction yields an exact optimum relation and shows that the problem is APX-hard. An example also exhibits a strict integrality gap for the natural linear programming relaxation.
item.dc:creator: Yuan Zhang, Jintao Zhang, Yun Feng

item.title: Weak and Strong Data Informativity with Structural Priors for System Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.38459v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When measurement data are insufficient for unique system identification, data informativity evaluates whether a dataset determines a property across all systems consistent with the data. This paper introduces a unified framework distinguishing between weak and strong data informativity under prior structural knowledge described by affine constraints: data are weakly informative if at least one system consistent with the data and prior knowledge possesses the target property, and strongly informative if every consistent system satisfies it. The latter is consistent with the notion of data informativity in the existing literature. By explicitly parameterizing all consistent systems as affine functions of free parameters via the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, we characterize these notions for fundamental system properties-including controllability, stabilizability, and stability. This formulation establishes that verifying weak and strong informativity, when tractable, reduces to rank tests of matrix pencils constructed from the data and prior knowledge. Our findings show that structural priors can lower data-excitation requirements and enable reliable analysis even when data fail to be strongly informative. Finally, the framework is extended to a class of noisy data.
item.dc:creator: Yuan Zhang, Wenxuan Xu, Yun Feng, Keke Huang, Keyou You

item.title: Knowledge Based Wind Turbine Gearbox Fault Detection Using Sparse Filtering and Graph Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2303.03496v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reliable gearbox condition monitoring requires methods that can process high-frequency vibration measurements while retaining information about sensor locations and drivetrain structure. We investigate a two-stage framework that combines sparse filtering with graph neural networks for wind turbine gearbox fault detection. Sparse filtering learns compact features from vibration segments, and a knowledge-based graph associates these features with gearbox components, sensors, and health-state entities. A basic graph neural network and a gated graph neural network produce a single health prediction, whereas a gated graph sequence neural network generates structured sequences that associate a predicted state with component and sensor information. Experiments use eight accelerometer channels from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory gearbox condition-monitoring benchmark. With 100 learned features, the sparse-filtering gated graph neural network achieves a reported classification accuracy of 93.74%, compared with 89.28% for its manually engineered feature counterpart. The sequence model achieves reported accuracies of 90.73% and 90.36% in the one- and two-fault-signal cases, respectively. These results support the use of learned vibration representations within a structured sensor graph. The evidence is restricted to the evaluated benchmark and operating condition; independent component localization, transfer across turbines, and deployment latency require further validation.
item.dc:creator: Jinsong Wang, Kenneth A. Loparo

item.title: Unbeatable imitation of a friend
item.description: arXiv:2507.16221v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Imitation sometimes achieves success in multi-agent situations even though it is very simple. In repeated games, success of imitation has been characterized by unbeatability against other agents. Previous studies specified conditions under which imitation is unbeatable against co-players in repeated symmetric games, and clarified that the existence of unbeatable imitation is strongly related to the existence of payoff-controlling strategies, called zero-determinant strategies. However, these results were on the situations in which one repeated game is played by one group of players. It was pointed out that imitation of other players in the same group and imitation of other players in the same role in other groups generally result in different outcomes. Here, we investigate the existence condition of unbeatable imitation in the latter situations, described by two concurrent repeated games played by two different groups of players. We find that the existence condition of unbeatable imitation is stronger than the existence condition of unbeatable zero-determinant strategies, whereas both are very limited. Furthermore, we find that adding exploration can make an imitation strategy unbeatable even in games where imitation without exploration can be beaten. Our findings suggest a strong relation between unbeatable imitation and payoff control even in the two concurrent repeated game situations.
item.dc:creator: Masahiko Ueda

item.title: A Survey of Freshness-Aware Wireless Networking with Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2512.21412v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The age of information (AoI) has become a central measure of data freshness in modern wireless systems. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising approach to AoI optimization, enabling adaptive decision-making in dynamic and stochastic wireless environments without requiring precise system models. Yet existing surveys either focus on classical AoI formulations or provide broad discussions of RL in wireless networks without addressing freshness as a unified learning problem. Motivated by this gap, this survey examines RL specifically through the lens of AoI and generalized freshness optimization. Motivated by this gap, this survey examines RL specifically through the lens of AoI and generalized freshness optimization. We organize AoI and its variants into native, function-based, and application-oriented families, providing a clearer view of how freshness should be modeled in B5G and 6G systems. Building on this foundation, we introduce a policy-centric taxonomy that reflects the decisions most relevant to freshness, consisting of update-control RL, medium-access RL, risk-sensitive RL, and multi-agent RL. This structure provides a coherent framework for understanding how learning can support important wireless networking problems, including sampling, scheduling, UAV trajectory planning, medium access, and distributed coordination. We further synthesize recent progress in RL-driven freshness control and highlight open challenges. The goal is to establish a unified foundation for learning-based freshness optimization in next-generation wireless networks.

item.title: Mixture-of-Models: Distributed Inference over Heterogeneous LLMs as Model-Level Mixture-of-Experts
item.description: arXiv:2601.16863v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Switch Transformers scale MoE model capacity by routing tokens in memory for one jointly trained model, requiring high-bandwidth interconnects, large memory, centralised ownership, and lack scalable composability. We propose Mixture-of-Models (MoM) architecture as Switch Transformer scaling to semantic level which composes inference across independently trained distributed LLMs, each run on its own GPU. The models reach joint consensus using N-Way Self-Evaluating Deliberation protocol: a combination of social-choice methods such as Delphi method and Quadratic Voting as well as Inference-Time scaling paradigm. We start with an empirical model that characterizes consensus as an inference-time trade-off between signal extraction and contextual noise accumulation, establishing a mathematical basis for convergence driven inference stopping strategies. We show experimental results where ensemble of smaller (<21B) models matches closely 120B MoE (GPT-OSS-120B) on AIME 2025 while larger ensemble of open-weight models reaches 90.0%, close to proprietary models at time of writing.
item.dc:creator: Tims Pecerskis, Aivars Smirnovs

item.title: How to Peel with a Knife: Aligning Fine-Grained Manipulation with Human Preference
item.description: arXiv:2603.03280v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many essential manipulation tasks - such as food preparation, surgery, and craftsmanship - remain difficult for autonomous robots. These tasks are characterized not only by contact-rich, force-sensitive dynamics, but also by their "implicit" success criteria: unlike pick-and-place, task quality in these domains is continuous and subjective (e.g. how well a potato is peeled), making quantitative evaluation and reward design difficult. We present a learning framework for such tasks, using peeling with a knife as a representative example. Our approach follows a two-stage pipeline: first, we learn a robust initial policy via force-aware data collection and imitation learning, enabling generalization across object variations; second, we refine the policy through preference-based finetuning using a learned reward model that combines quantitative task metrics with qualitative human feedback, aligning policy behavior with human-evaluated task quality. Using only 50~200 peeling trajectories, our system achieves 100% same-produce success on cucumbers, apples, and potatoes, with performance improving by up to 40% through preference-based finetuning. Remarkably, policies trained on one produce category also transfer zero-shot to selected held-out produce categories, achieving 50% success on zucchini, 90% on pear, and 80% on daikon radish.
item.dc:creator: Toru Lin, Shuying Deng, Zhao-Heng Yin, Pieter Abbeel, Jitendra Malik

item.title: Minimizing the Age of Incorrect Information of Discrete-Time Markov Sources With Hybrid ARQ
item.description: arXiv:2603.28369v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This work introduces a framework for analyzing the Age of Incorrect Information (AoII) in a real-time monitoring system with a generic discrete-time Markov source. We study a noisy communication system employing a hybrid automatic repeat request (HARQ) protocol, subject to a transmission rate constraint. The optimization problem is formulated as a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP), and it is shown that there exists an optimal policy that is a randomized mixture of two stationary policies. To overcome the intractability of computing the optimal stationary policies, we develop a multiple-threshold policy class where thresholds depend on the source, the receiver, and the packet count. By establishing a Markov renewal structure induced by threshold policies, we derive closed-form expressions for the long-term average AoII and transmission rate. The proposed policy is constructed via a relative value iteration algorithm that leverages the threshold structure to skip computations, combined with a bisection search to satisfy the rate constraint. To accommodate scenarios requiring lower computational complexity, we adapt the same technique to produce a simpler single-threshold policy that trades optimality for efficiency. Numerical experiments exhibit that both thresholdbased policies outperform periodic scheduling, with the multiplethreshold approach matching the performance of the globally optimal policy.
item.dc:creator: Konstantinos Bountrogiannis, Anthony Ephremides, Panagiotis Tsakalides, George Tzagkarakis

item.title: MERIS: Adaptive Real-Time Scheduling of Refined Inference DAGs in Dynamic Robotic Environments
item.description: arXiv:2605.24044v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robots deployed in dynamic environments execute changing directed-acyclic-graph (DAG) workloads under limited compute and timing budgets. This article presents MERIS, a framework for model scheduling under real-time constraints that combines proportional intermediate deadlines, MIMONet-aware graph refinement, and event-driven synchronization for multi-task inference on resource-constrained robotic platforms. We distinguish three representations: the application DAG, each MIMONet's internal encoder/decoder graph, and the refined scheduling DAG, and make the scope of the timing argument explicit. If the profiled execution bounds, release assumptions, precedence barriers, and per-level capacity premises hold, satisfaction of the assigned sub-deadlines composes to the end-to-end deadline. For non-partitionable tasks, we define a profile-bounded admission rule; before interpreting that rule as empirical timing evidence, we require direct per-task completion checks. We report run-level QoE alongside the offered-node deadline missing rate, making explicit that run completion and successful service of every node are different outcomes. We propose a comprehensive minibenchmark for evaluating the performance of schedulers under various DNN-driven autonomous driving scenarios. Extensive experiments on Nano Orin, AGX Orin, and M3 Max demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.
item.dc:creator: Zexin Li, Tao Ren, Johnathan Liu, Xiaoxi He, Cong Liu

item.title: Lifted Schr\"odinger Bridges for Gaussian Mixture Endpoints: Projection Gaps and Path-Space Obstructions
item.description: arXiv:2605.24795v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study stochastic density control between Gaussian-mixture endpoint distributions under Brownian prior dynamics. Since the direct Schr\"odinger bridge between Gaussian mixtures is generally not available in closed form, we introduce a lifted path-space construction in which each trajectory is augmented with a source--target component label. Consequently, the problem decomposes into Gaussian component-to-component Schr\"odinger bridges with explicit marginal, drift, and cost formulas, while the mixture-level assignment reduces to a finite-dimensional entropic coupling problem with a Sinkhorn scaling form. We then analyze the projection obtained by discarding or forgetting the label. By construction, the projected law satisfies the original Gaussian-mixture endpoint constraints, but its relative entropy generally differs from the lifted relative entropy by a nonnegative conditional label-information gap. This gap reveals a path-space obstruction: the lifted optimizer cannot, in general, be identified with the direct unlabeled Schr\"odinger bridge after projection. We also derive the posterior-averaged Markov drift associated with the projected marginal flow, prove a kinetic-energy upper bound, and identify a common path-potential condition under which the projection gap vanishes. Several numerical illustrations showing density and shape control are recorded for a self-contained exposition.
item.dc:creator: Siddhartha Ganguly, George Rapakoulias, Panagiotis Tsiotras

item.title: When Should a Robot Replan? Regret-Guided Update Scheduling in Time-Varying MDPs
item.description: arXiv:2606.16972v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robots operating in non-stationary environments must continually adapt their policies as the dynamics drift, but onboard energy and compute budgets cap how often a full state estimation and re-planning step can be performed. This raises a question: \emph{when}, along a horizon, should a robot spend its limited budget? We formulate this problem in time-varying Markov decision processes (TVMDPs) with a known bound on the rate of transition drift. We model execution as a \emph{skip-update} scheme in which, at chosen update times, the agent estimates the transition kernel by maximum likelihood and computes a finite-horizon policy, and between updates reuses this policy under a propagated state estimate. We analyze the dynamic regret of this scheme and show how it grows during skip intervals in terms of the properties of the TVMDP and the skip lengths; the resulting bound answers the opening question via an online, regret-guided update rule that allocates the budget adaptively. We evaluate the rule in a simulated Mars-rover navigation task with time-varying slip dynamics and on a Crazyflie quadrotor in indoor obstacle fields. Adaptive allocation outperforms other budgeted baselines.
item.dc:creator: Negin Musavi, Gokul Puthumanaillam, Ruben Hernandez, William Schafer, Melkior Ornik

item.title: SEAMLiS: Visibility-Aware Safety for Perception-Limited Multi-Robot Exploration
item.description: arXiv:2607.09959v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Autonomous exploration in unknown environments is typically driven by informative frontiers, viewpoints, or trajectories, while local safety controllers avoid obstacles represented in the current map. Under finite sensing range and limited field of view, this separation can be unsafe: an exploration stack may plan optimistically through unobserved space and steer the sensor toward information gain rather than along the direction of motion, causing hidden obstacles to be detected too late for bounded-actuation avoidance. This paper presents SEAMLiS (Safe Exploration for Autonomous Multi-Robot Systems Under Limited Sensing), a modular execution-layer safety framework for decentralized multi-robot exploration. SEAMLiS preserves the upstream exploration stack, including the goal allocator and local planner, and enforces safety at the execution layer through perception-aware attitude and positional filters. A gatekeeper-based attitude filter switches between a visibility-promoting yaw policy and a velocity-tracking backup policy to preserve visibility of the critical known-free/unknown boundary with sufficient braking margin. A Control Barrier Function (CBF)-based positional filter then avoids known obstacles, newly detected obstacles, and other robots. We provide sufficient collision-avoidance conditions and validate the framework in randomized simulation, Isaac Sim, and Crazyflie hardware experiments. Results show collision-free exploration across tested single- and multi-robot settings while retaining much of the efficiency of visibility-promoting yaw control.
item.dc:creator: Taekyung Kim, Rahul H Kumar, Aswin D. Menon, Tzu-Hsiang Lin, Dimitra Panagou

item.title: BarrierFormer: Transformer-Guided Predictive Barrier Enforcement for Safe Robot Control
item.description: arXiv:2609.23896v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) have become one of the most popular tools for encoding and enforcing state constraints in safety-critical robotics. Standard CBF approaches are inherently myopic in nature as they enforce safety only at the current time step. Consequently, the system can be driven toward the boundary of the safe set where no feasible safe control exists at a future timestep. Model predictive control (MPC) based approaches address this by enforcing state constraints over a receding horizon. However, such approaches generally require the model to be known for solving a constrained optimization problem at every step, which is computationally expensive for real-time deployment. We propose BarrierFormer, a barrier-supervised transformer framework that addresses these limitations by encoding rollout-level CBF constraints in learning a model-free safe policy. A causal transformer encodes observation-action history, autoregressively generates a predictive rollout through the dynamics head to replace the model, and provides a residual correction to a nominal controller through the action head to replace the online computation. A barrier critic operating on local observations evaluates CBF constraint violations along this rollout, and a safety teacher computes barrier-consistent actions satisfying these constraints as direct supervision targets for the learned control policy. During inference, the policy maps observation-action history to control actions without any online optimization or model knowledge, enabling real-time model-free predictive safety enforcement. Evaluations across linear and nonlinear, 2D and 3D dynamical systems for safe goal-directed navigation demonstrate that BarrierFormer outperforms existing reinforcement learning (RL)-based, diffusion-based, MPC-based, and transformer-based approaches in safety rate and inference latency.
item.dc:creator: Anandsingh Chauhan, Kunal Garg

item.title: DiffGIPC: Differentiable Mixed-Coordinate Contact Mechanics on GPU
item.description: arXiv:2610.19091v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Contact-rich inverse problems require efficient gradients and reliable enforcement of non-penetration. Existing differentiable methods provide fast simulation and rigid-deformable coupling, but contact treatments based on penalties or velocity-level constraints can permit penetration or positional drift. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) maintains non-penetration through geometric barriers and {continuous collision detection (CCD)}. However, repeated forward and backward evaluations remain costly in full-space finite-element (FEM) implementations, particularly when nearly rigid components retain many vertex {degrees of freedom (DoFs)}. We present DiffGIPC, a GPU-accelerated differentiable IPC framework for optimizing interacting deformable and nearly rigid bodies. Our affine-body derivatives enable {rest-shape} design, initial-state optimization, and articulated control while retaining only twelve motion DoFs per affine body. These gradients account for how changes in geometry, placement, and actuation affect other objects through collision and friction. We preserve these interactions in one coupled FEM-affine adjoint system per frame, reducing the backward-system size without discarding the dependencies that drive the inverse problem. GPU-optimized backward computation further reduces the cost of repeated gradient evaluations. A reusable PyTorch interface connects supported physical parameters to user-defined parameter maps and losses across design, identification, motion, placement, and articulated control. Experiments demonstrate peak speedups over DiffIPC of approximately 150.0x with full-space FEM and 4133.3x with affine bodies for combined forward simulation and backward differentiation.
item.dc:creator: Kemeng Huang, Bowen Ren, Xinyu Lu, Minchen Li, Taku komura

item.title: Autonomous fixed-wing interception using reinforcement learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.37470v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.
item.dc:creator: Daan van Hamersveld, Ewoud Smeur, Iurii Kriachko
